source: Friedman et al. (2026) Not Too Short, Not Too Long: How LLM Response Length Shapes People's Critical Thinking in Error Detection
finding: Only study found that uses Watson-Glaser items together with an LLM. People judged whether a GPT-5 explanation of a Watson-Glaser item was correct. People copied the LLM's error when its answer was wrong.
numbers: N=24 within-subjects. 15 modified Watson-Glaser items, 3 per facet (inference, assumptions, deduction, interpretation, argument evaluation). 8 LLM outputs correct, 7 with planted errors in the final conclusion only. Output length 42-150 words (M=82.2). Outputs made with ChatGPT default model (GPT-5), Aug 2025.
limits: Workshop paper, 6 pages. Small N. One LLM. The task was judging the LLM, not solving the item. Items were modified, not the official test. Length was varied by editing.
agent_relevance: Shows Watson-Glaser items can be turned into an LLM-error-detection probe. Useful template for a gate that checks whether a critic can spot a wrong conclusion behind sound-looking steps.

source: Friedman et al. (2026) Not Too Short, Not Too Long (Table 1 and interaction)
finding: When the LLM was wrong, human accuracy was low unless the explanation was medium length. When the LLM was right, accuracy was high at every length.
numbers: Model-estimated P(correct): LLM incorrect short 0.245 [0.127,0.422], medium 0.542 [0.362,0.713], long 0.307 [0.169,0.491]. LLM correct short 0.715, medium 0.811, long 0.795.
limits: Mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercept for question. Only 7 error items. Non-monotonic length effect is from a small sample and may not replicate.
agent_relevance: Longer or shorter text does not protect a reader from a confident wrong conclusion. Supports G5: do not let a judge be swayed by length or fluent steps; check the conclusion by code.

source: Friedman et al. (2026) Not Too Short, Not Too Long (open-ended answers)
finding: Participants often trusted the LLM's step-by-step reasoning even when the final yes/no conclusion was wrong. The planted error sat only in the conclusion.
numbers: Qualitative coding of written rationales; no percentage reported in the sections read.
limits: Early qualitative look only. The paper says it does not measure underlying cognitive processes.
agent_relevance: A step-by-step trace that looks sound is not evidence that the answer is right. Same lesson as G2/G3: check the final answer against real output, not against the trace.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Evaluating the Logical Reasoning Ability of ChatGPT and GPT-4
finding: On exam-derived logic tests (civil-service LogiQA, LSAT-based ReClor and AR-LSAT) GPT-4 beat ChatGPT and a fine-tuned RoBERTa on familiar sets, but fell on new sets. On AR-LSAT, GPT-4 via API was far below the human average.
numbers: Accuracy %. LogiQA 2.0 test: human avg 86, ceiling 95, RoBERTa 48.76, ChatGPT 52.37, GPT-4 API 72.25. ReClor dev: human 63, ceiling 100, RoBERTa 55.01, ChatGPT 57.38, GPT-4 API 87.20. AR-LSAT: human 56, ceiling 91, RoBERTa 23.14, ChatGPT 20.42, GPT-4 API 33.48. LogiQA 2.0 out-of-distribution (2022 exam): human 83, ceiling 99, ChatGPT 38.44, GPT-4 API 58.49.
limits: Table says ChatGPT 52.37 on LogiQA 2.0 test but the text says 53.37. GPT-4 chat-UI numbers come from about 100 items per set. ReClor GPT-4 87.2 may be inflated by training exposure to old LSAT items.
agent_relevance: Official-exam logic items are the nearest usable stand-in for Watson-Glaser/CCTST items. The out-of-distribution drop (72 to 58) says the S0 gate must use items the model cannot have seen.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Evaluating the Logical Reasoning Ability of ChatGPT and GPT-4 (context and CoT tests)
finding: GPT-4 scored higher when 20 items were asked in one conversation than when each was asked in a fresh window. Adding 'Let's think step by step' raised GPT-4 on the out-of-distribution set.
numbers: LogiQA 2.0 ood, 20 items: 9 correct in same window, 5 in new windows. ConTRoL, 20 items: 13 vs 7. CoT on 112 ood items: 61 correct vs 54 without CoT (48.21%).
limits: Tiny samples (20 items). No significance tests. One run.
agent_relevance: Item order and shared context change scores. The S0 gate and our logs should run each item in a clean context, or the gate measures carry-over, not skill.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Evaluating the Logical Reasoning Ability of ChatGPT and GPT-4 (NLI tests)
finding: On logic-heavy natural language inference sets the gain over a fine-tuned RoBERTa was small. GPT-4 did not follow the label format steadily.
numbers: ChatGPT: ConTRoL 58.45, ConjNLI 47.03, HELP 42.31, MED 55.02, TaxiNLI 57.30, MNLI dev 55.40. GPT-4: ConTRoL 56.40, ConjNLI 72.71, MED 89.42, HELP 46.01, TaxiNLI 60.08, MNLI dev 64.08.
limits: Instruction-following noise mixed with reasoning. One run per set.
agent_relevance: Output-format failure looks like reasoning failure. The gate should parse answers in code and count format failures separately.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) AGIEval: A Human-Centric Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models
finding: On human admission exams (LSAT, SAT, LogiQA, Gaokao) GPT-4 passed the average human on LSAT logical reasoning and reading, but stayed far below the top human, and was weak on LSAT analytical reasoning. Zero-shot CoT did not help GPT-4 on LSAT.
numbers: Accuracy %. Human avg / top: LSAT-AR 56/91, LSAT-LR 56/91, LSAT-RC 56/91, LogiQA-en 86/95. GPT-4 zero-shot: LSAT-AR 35.2, LSAT-LR 80.6, LSAT-RC 85.9, LogiQA-en 49.3. GPT-4 zero-shot CoT: LSAT-AR 34.4, LSAT-LR 80.6, LSAT-RC 85.1, LogiQA-en 57.8. GPT-4 few-shot LogiQA-en 63.9. ChatGPT zero-shot LSAT-LR 52.6.
limits: Human averages for LSAT/SAT/Gaokao were estimated by scaling scores. Public exam items may be in training data. Few-shot examples used ChatGPT-written explanations.
agent_relevance: The LSAT-LR type (weaken, strengthen, assumption, flaw) is the closest published LLM benchmark to Watson-Glaser/CCTST skills. CoT adding nothing on LSAT-LR means we should not assume a reasoning scaffold helps there; test it (G7).

source: Zhong et al. (2023) AGIEval (averages and prompt effects)
finding: Across 20 tasks GPT-4 beats ChatGPT by a wide margin, but CoT effect is task-dependent: it helps math, barely moves GPT-4 on language and logic exams.
numbers: Average over tasks: human avg 67, top 91. Zero-shot GPT-4 56.4, zero-shot CoT 58.4. Few-shot GPT-4 about 59.2, few-shot CoT 61.3. ChatGPT zero-shot 42.9, zero-shot CoT 43.2.
limits: Averages mix math and language tasks. Model versions were those on Azure in early 2023.
agent_relevance: Gains from prompt scaffolds are small and uneven. The schema should measure scaffold gain per item type, not on a mixed average.

source: Wang et al. (2022) From LSAT: The Progress and Challenges of Complex Reasoning
finding: An older, pre-ChatGPT system built for the LSAT: separate neural-symbolic modules for analytical reasoning, logical reasoning and reading comprehension reached the human median overall.
numbers: Overall accuracy 56.8% on LSAT exams, said to be comparable to the median human test taker. Reading and logical reasoning modules claimed to reach top-30 and top-58 law-school admission levels.
limits: Claims are from the abstract and introduction of an older system. Admission-level claims depend on score mapping. Not re-tested on newer models here.
agent_relevance: Shows an exam-targeted pipeline (parse constraints to programs, then solve) already matched median humans in 2022. Same idea as our rule that code does the selecting (G5).

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: Agent loop that turns an LSAT-style problem into a formal form, runs a solver, and refines on solver errors. Beat standard prompting and CoT on all five sets. On AR-LSAT, CoT was no better than plain prompting.
numbers: Accuracy %, Standard / CoT / Logic-LM. AR-LSAT: ChatGPT 20.34/17.31/26.41; GPT-3.5 22.51/22.51/25.54; GPT-4 33.33/35.06/43.04. LogicalDeduction GPT-4 71.33/75.25/87.63. FOLIO GPT-4 69.11/70.58/78.92. Avg gain with GPT-3.5: +39.2 over standard, +18.4 over CoT. CoT effect on AR-LSAT -3.2 on average.
limits: Un-executable formal forms fall back to CoT. AR-LSAT test has 231 items, so a 1-point change is about 2 items. Gains smaller on AR-LSAT than on rule-based sets.
agent_relevance: Direct example of an exam-type task inside an agent loop with a program checking the answer. Supports G2/G3: revise from solver output, not opinion. Also shows CoT is not a free win.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM (self-refinement)
finding: Self-refinement from solver error messages made more formal forms executable, but accuracy stopped rising after the first rounds.
numbers: Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 on average. On AR-LSAT with GPT-4 the executable rate went from about 32.6 to 39.8 percent in the Table 3 comparison. Accuracy 'tends to stagnate' in later rounds on FOLIO.
limits: Feedback was only syntax error messages, not logic errors. Numbers read from a flattened PDF table; check against paper before quoting precisely.
agent_relevance: Revision helps when the signal is concrete (G2). It does not help once the feedback carries no information about the logic. Cap refinement rounds.

source: Yu et al. (2020) ReClor: A Reading Comprehension Dataset Requiring Logical Reasoning
finding: Dataset of 6,138 GMAT/LSAT logical reasoning items with question types such as necessary assumption, weaken, strengthen, identify a flaw. Models exploited answer-option biases: good on the EASY (biased) split, poor on HARD.
numbers: 91.22% of items from real GMAT and LSAT exams. Fine-tuned models about 75% on EASY, about 30% on HARD. Even RACE-then-ReClor RoBERTa-large was only about 50% on HARD. Ten graduate students each took 10 random items; the human average of 63 on ReClor dev is quoted in c04.
limits: Human baseline is 10 students on 100 items, so it is noisy; the paper itself warns the EASY/HARD human gap may be small-sample. 2020 models only.
agent_relevance: Gives item types that match Watson-Glaser facets (assumption, evaluation of arguments, inference). The EASY/HARD split is a model to copy: report scores on items where option-only guessing fails.

source: Liu et al. (2020) LogiQA: A Challenge Dataset for Machine Reading Comprehension with Logical Reasoning
finding: Dataset from Chinese civil-service exam logic items, tagged by five reasoning types (categorical, sufficient and necessary conditional, disjunctive, conjunctive). Fine-tuned models were far below humans.
numbers: Test set 867 items. Best model (RoBERTa) 35.31%. Humans 86.00% (three postgraduate students, 500 items), ceiling 96.00%. Category shares: categorical 30.8%, sufficient conditional 27.6%, necessary conditional 24.7%.
limits: Pre-2023 models. Translated to English. Human sample is three people.
agent_relevance: Lets us tag our logs by reasoning type. Later models rose from 35% to 72% (c04), so this set is near saturated for strong models and weak as a gate.

source: OpenAI (2023) GPT-4 Technical Report
finding: GPT-4 scored at the 88th percentile on the LSAT, GPT-3.5 at about the 40th. Authors ran contamination checks and report the lower of two scores.
numbers: LSAT score: GPT-4 163 (~88th percentile), GPT-4 no vision 161 (~83rd), GPT-3.5 149 (~40th). Rule: for each exam run a variant with seen questions removed and report the lower score.
limits: Exam setups vary; some problems were seen in training. Percentiles map from public score tables. LSAT multiple choice only partly separated from contamination.
agent_relevance: A single-number percentile anchor for the logic-test skill of frontier models. Also a method: report the lower of contaminated and cleaned scores.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models and humans both judged syllogisms and Wason tasks better when content matched real-world belief. This is the belief-bias effect that critical-thinking tests such as Watson-Glaser deduction items and Cornell try to measure.
numbers: Three tasks (NLI, syllogism validity, Wason). Wason: humans not above chance overall. Realistic-rule advantage significant for humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (all z>2.2, p<0.03); marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (z about 1.78, p about 0.08). Humans slower than 80 s (top 15%) were above chance only on the Realistic condition.
limits: Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2 variants, GPT-3.5, not current frontier models. Scoring used log-probabilities with a correction. New items were written to avoid contamination.
agent_relevance: Checks a model for belief bias with same-logic, different-content item pairs. Good design for an S0 gate probe and for our logs: score logic-equal pairs, not single items.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects (response time link)
finding: In humans, slower answers were more accurate on the Wason task; longer thinking helped. Models showed related patterns between answer confidence and human response time.
numbers: Human accuracy vs response time on Wason: z=4.44, p<0.001. Slow group = top 15% of times, over 80 seconds.
limits: Correlational. Time on task confounds with effort and attention.
agent_relevance: Human test data say spending more time helps on belief-conflict items, but the gain was on Realistic items only. Suggests extra thinking budget should be spent only after a conflict signal (G1).

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: Fallacy detection (a Cornell/Watson-Glaser-adjacent skill) was hard for 12 pretrained language models. A structure-aware classifier beat the best language model.
numbers: 12 models scored 8.62% to 53.31% micro F1 on LOGIC (13 fallacy types; best language model Electra 53.31). Structure-aware Electra 58.77 F1, +5.46 over Electra; +4.51 on LOGICCLIMATE. Zero-shot classifiers were close to the random baseline. Most frequent class: faulty generalization 18.01%.
quote: existing pretrained large language models perform poorly on this task
limits: Pre-ChatGPT models. Only 2022 encoders and early GPT models; no frontier chat models tested.
agent_relevance: Gives a labeled fallacy set for our logs. Result is old; re-run on current models before using it as a gate.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2022/2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Cognitive Reflection Test (a test of resisting a lure) and semantic illusions across GPT models and 500 humans. Pre-ChatGPT models fell for the lure more than humans. ChatGPT models solved most items by writing out steps.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks, 500 Prolific participants. Correct: GPT-3 davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%, humans 38%. Intuitive (lure) answers: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Semantic illusions correct: davinci-003 18%, ChatGPT-3.5 74%, ChatGPT-4 88%, humans 26%.
limits: Authors' own CRT-style items, partly auto-generated. Text gives 96% in one place and 95% in another for ChatGPT-4. Items may now be in training data.
agent_relevance: Humans and weak models fail lure items at similar rates; strong chat models do not. A CRT-type probe is an easy S0 check that the model is not answering on the first impulse.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs (prompt manipulations)
finding: A small prompt change moved a weak model a lot. A reflective instruction and a few worked examples each raised accuracy. Blocking step-by-step output removed much of the ChatGPT advantage.
numbers: davinci-003: 'Let us use algebra to solve this problem' CRT correct 5% to 28%, atypical answers 15% to 43%. Training examples: CRT Type 2 accuracy 2% to 92% after two examples; Type 3 12% to 92% after seven. Semantic illusions: suffix 'Think carefully and check the question for invalid assumptions' 18% to 54%; with 10+ examples over 64%. Forbidding CoT for ChatGPT models cut chain-of-thought responses from 97% to 0% (3.5) and 84% to 0% (4).
limits: Single model for most manipulations. Chi-square tests across prompt conditions, not across many runs.
agent_relevance: The 'check for invalid assumptions' suffix is a Watson-Glaser 'recognition of assumptions' move used as a prompt. It helped a weak model but G1 warns against always-on doubt on strong ones; test per model.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 answered all three Cognitive Reflection Test items with the intuitive wrong answer. On 12 vignette problems it gave human-like answers in all 12 but was correct on only six.
numbers: CRT 1-3: 0 of 3 correct. 12 vignettes (e.g. Linda problem): 6 correct, 12 human-like.
limits: One 2022 model, three CRT items. Vignettes were famous and may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Early baseline against which c18 shows the abrupt change with chat models. Famous test items are likely memorised; use fresh items.

source: Zhai, Nyaaba and Ma (2024) Can generative AI and ChatGPT outperform humans on cognitive-demanding problem-solving tasks in science?
finding: ChatGPT and GPT-4 on 54 NAEP science items beat most students who got each item right. Human difficulty rose with task cognitive demand; model performance did not track it, except at Grade 4.
numbers: Median share of students scoring below the model: ChatGPT 83%, 70%, 81% at Grades 4, 8, 12; GPT-4 74%, 71%, 81%. Same answer from both models on 90%, 75%, 94% of items. Kendall tau-b between required student ability and cognitive demand at Grade 12: .513, p=.008.
limits: Student rank is estimated from item-level percentages because student data were restricted. 54 items. Models may have seen released NAEP items.
agent_relevance: A published method for placing an LLM on a human standardised-test scale from item statistics. Also shows model difficulty does not follow human difficulty, so human norms may not transfer to the S0 gate.

source: Castagna, Sassoon and Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying
finding: An agent pipeline that is close to a critical-thinking rubric: draft a reasoning plan, ask eight critical questions about premises, warrants and conclusions, loop until enough answers are positive, then answer. It beat plain and CoT on MT-Bench reasoning and math for most of five models.
numbers: 8 critical questions; pass at 7/8 yes, relaxed to 5/8 after 5 iterations, forced after 10. MT-Bench reasoning (1-10), Standard/CoT/CQoT: Llama 3.1-70b 8.05/7.5/8.4; Gemini 1.5-pro 8.45/8.25/8.9; GPT-4o 8.3/8.2/8.45; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 8.6/8.55/8.95; Nemotron-51b 6.75/7.7/7.3. Math: GPT-4o 9.5/8.95/9.6. CQoT best or joint best on 19 of 20 comparisons.
limits: MT-Bench is small (about 20 items per category) and scored by an LLM judge. The model answers its own critical questions, so checks are not independent. Nemotron CQoT below CoT on reasoning.
agent_relevance: Closest existing use of test-style critical-thinking checks inside an LLM loop. Conflicts with G1 and G2 on two points: it questions on a schedule, and the model grades itself. Needs an equal-token test (G7) before borrowing.

source: Castagna, Sassoon and Parsons (2024) CQoT ablation
finding: Removing the critical-question step lowered scores. Plan-then-answer alone gave part of the gain.
numbers: MT-Bench reasoning, Standard / Step 1+4 only / full CQoT: Llama 3.1-70b 8.05 / 8.3 / 8.4; Nemotron-51b 6.75 / 6.85 / 7.3.
limits: Two models only. Differences of 0.1 to 0.5 points on a 10-point judged scale with small n.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain may come from planning before answering, not from the critique. Our schema should test plan-only against plan-plus-critique at equal tokens.

source: Tak et al. (2026) Sparks of Rationality: Do Reasoning LLMs Align with Human Judgment and Choice?
finding: Across several LLM families, deliberate 'thinking' reliably improved rationality on choice-axiom benchmarks. Emotion steering shifted answers, and the same reasoning that raised rationality also made models more steerable.
numbers: No single headline number read in the abstract and introduction. Compares in-context priming and representation-level steering.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read closely. About choice rationality, not critical-thinking tests.
agent_relevance: Weak link to this subfield. Suggests a gate that checks critical thinking must also test for being pushed by emotional framing.

source: Gap statement from this session's search (no source)
finding: No paper was found that scores an LLM on the official Watson-Glaser, Cornell or CCTST. The only Watson-Glaser LLM paper found was c01. Surrogate tests (LSAT, LogiQA, ReClor, CRT) fill the gap.
numbers: arXiv title and abstract searches for 'Watson-Glaser' returned 1 hit (c01). OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited and the shared WebSearch budget was used up, so coverage is incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search. Test publishers keep items proprietary, which would reduce open papers anyway.
agent_relevance: Our S0 gate should rely on open surrogate sets with fresh variants, and log item type. Re-search later with a working Scholar index.

source: Synthesis across c04, c07, c10, c14 (LSAT-style items)
finding: Same task family, wide range of model scores depending on item type and prompt. Reading and logical-reasoning items are near or above human average. Analytical-reasoning (constraint) items stay low for plain prompting and improve most when a solver is added.
numbers: GPT-4: LSAT-LR 80.6 and LSAT-RC 85.9 zero-shot vs human avg 56 (AGIEval); AR-LSAT 33.3 plain to 43.0 with solver (Logic-LM); LSAT 163 (~88th percentile) overall (GPT-4 report).
limits: Different model versions and test splits across papers; numbers are not directly comparable. Mixed run settings.
agent_relevance: A scaffold gain shows up on constraint-type items where code can check, not on argument-evaluation items. Split the gate by item type.

source: Synthesis across c18, c19, c20 and c15 (lure and belief-bias items)
finding: Trap items that catch humans caught weak or older models even more, then stopped catching chat models once they wrote out steps. This tracks the capability level, not the item.
numbers: CRT correct: GPT-3 0 of 3 (Binz) and 5% (Hagendorff); ChatGPT-3.5 59%; ChatGPT-4 96%; humans 38%. Wason: no model or human above chance overall on abstract rules (Lampinen).
limits: Items are public and may be memorised by newer models. Wason results come from older models.
agent_relevance: Lure items are a cheap low-cost check at S0 but go stale fast; build a rotating generator and log the item source.

source: Synthesis across c01, c03, c22 (human reading LLM reasoning)
finding: Humans checking LLM conclusions are fooled by sound-looking steps, and LLM self-critique with critical questions is also self-graded. Both rely on opinion rather than an outside check.
numbers: Human P(correct) when LLM wrong 0.245 (short), 0.542 (medium), 0.307 (long); CQoT pass rule 7 of 8 positive self-answers.
limits: Two different settings (human readers vs model self-critique), so no direct comparison of rates.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G2 and G5: a critic's yes/no on its own reasoning is weak evidence; require a code-checked failing output.
